Question: The number of real solutions \((x,y,z,w)\) of the simultaneous equations \[ \begin{aligned} 2y&=x+\frac{17}{x},\\ 2z&=y+\frac{17}{y},\\ 2w&=z+\frac{17}{z},\\ 2x&=w+\frac{17}{w}. \end{aligned} \] is
Solution:
Method 1: Bound the entries and close an inequality chain

The equations repeatedly apply the same rule
\[
f(t)=\frac{t+17/t}{2},\qquad t\ne0,
\]
and return to the starting value after four steps. If we find a range where each step can only decrease, returning to the start will force every step to be an equality.

All four variables must be nonzero because they occur in denominators. Also, \(t\) and \(17/t\) have the same sign, so \(f(t)\) has the sign of \(t\). The equations therefore force all four variables to have the same sign.

First suppose they are positive. For every \(t>0\), AM-GM gives
\[
f(t)=\frac{t+17/t}{2}
\ge\sqrt{t\cdot\frac{17}{t}}=\sqrt{17}.
\]
Every variable is an output of this rule, so all four are at least \(\sqrt{17}\). For \(t\ge\sqrt{17}\), we have \(17/t\le t\), and hence \(f(t)\le t\). Applying this to the four equations gives
\[
x\ge y\ge z\ge w\ge x.
\]
Thus all four values are equal. Calling their common positive value \(r\), the first equation becomes
\[
2r=r+\frac{17}{r},
\qquad r^2=17,
\]
so \(r=\sqrt{17}\).

If all four variables are negative, substituting their negatives produces positive numbers satisfying the same system. The positive-case result shows that the original entries must all equal \(-\sqrt{17}\).

Both constant tuples satisfy the original equations because \(17/t=t\) when \(t=\pm\sqrt{17}\). These are distinct, and the sign cases exhaust all possibilities. There are exactly \(\boxed{2}\) real solutions, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

Method 2: Turn each step into squaring

Let
\[
f(t)=\frac{t+17/t}{2},\qquad t\ne0,
\qquad r=\sqrt{17}.
\]
The value \(r\) is a natural reference because \(f(r)=r\). Factoring \(f(t)-r\) and \(f(t)+r\) will reveal a quantity whose behavior is especially simple under repeated steps.

First, every variable must be nonzero. Since \(f(t)\) has the same sign as \(t\), all four variables have the same sign. Consider the positive case.

For \(t>0\), using \(r^2=17\) gives
\[
f(t)-r=\frac{(t-r)^2}{2t},
\qquad
f(t)+r=\frac{(t+r)^2}{2t}.
\]
Thus, if we define
\[
q(t)=\frac{t-r}{t+r},\qquad t>0,
\]
then all denominators are positive and
\[
q(f(t))=q(t)^2.
\]
This quotient is useful because one application of the original rule becomes one squaring. The four equations consequently give
\[
q(y)=q(x)^2,\quad q(z)=q(y)^2,
\]
\[
q(w)=q(z)^2,\quad q(x)=q(w)^2.
\]
Writing \(u=q(x)\), we obtain \(u=u^{16}\). Because \(x,r>0\), we have \(-1<u<1\). The equation \(u=u^{16}\) forces \(u\ge0\), while \(0<u<1\) would imply \(u^{16}<u\). Therefore \(u=0\), which means \(x=r\). The original equations then force \(y=z=w=r\).

Negating all four entries preserves the system, so the all-negative case gives exactly the tuple with every entry \(-r\). Both constant tuples satisfy the equations, and mixed signs and zero entries have already been excluded. Hence there are exactly \(\boxed{2}\) solutions, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
